extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers and wartime news consumers
extracted.subtask_description: Contemporary newspaper reporting of World War II military operations, battles, and related official communiqués, including Q&A on how combat results (e.g., enemy aircraft destroyed) are determined and reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusive evidence for a destroyed enemy aircraft
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepted conclusive evidence requires a witness (gunner or other) to see the plane hit the land or sea; to see the plane explode/implode in the air; to see the pilot bail out (for single-seater fighters); or to see the plane dive away so completely enveloped in flames as to preclude any possibility of it being flown away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the specific criteria used by the checkers to list a plane as 'destroyed'. Examples given: seeing a plane hit the sea, seeing an in-air explosion, or observing a pilot parachute. If such direct observations exist, the loss is counted as destroyed.

rubrics_metrics.name: No credit when aircraft are lost to sight or possibly recoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: If a plane is seen apparently out of control but then disappears into cloud or otherwise is lost to sight, it is not listed as destroyed; similarly, a plane apparently on fire is not counted if there is any reasonable possibility the pilot could regain control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The policy stresses caution: planes not positively observed to crash/explode/bail out are not credited as destroyed because pilots may regain control or the aircraft may escape; this is an anti-pattern to avoid over-claiming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures to prevent duplication in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Because gunners from multiple aircraft can fire at the same enemy fighter and honestly report a kill, precautions are taken to prevent duplicate credits by checking times and other circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interrogating officers compare notes and check and double-check answers (times, locations, witness reports) to detect and remove duplicate claims. Preliminary higher figures are routinely adjusted downward after these checks. The article notes investigators take every precaution, although regulations may limit publication of checking details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences and cross-checking between RAF and USAAF accounting methods
rubrics_metrics.description: RAF methods of determining enemy losses long were regarded as conservative and accurate and differ from USAAF methods; when comparing figures the two forces' checking processes are used to reconcile counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Various interrogating officers and checking procedures are used to compare notes between services; despite methodological differences, cross-checks and reconciliations are performed so final announced totals reflect those adjudications. This explains why preliminary or private figures may be higher than the officially given numbers.
